probity_note: Halcyon Group, all named individuals (Maya Lindqvist, Dana Whitfield, the night-desk team leads) and every figure in the exhibit are fictional and were invented for assessment purposes. The marking model is an evidence map for human-anchored scoring, not an automated trait engine. Score judgement, not velocity.

diagnostic_acuity.description: Whether the candidate reads what the data actually says rather than what the dashboard framing suggests. Everything needed is on the exhibit; the sharper cuts (shift, roster) are retrievable from the Halcyon Knowledge System. Reward candidates who surface an issue and reason about it defensibly, even if framed differently from the expected wording.

embedded_issues.title: The 7.4 headline masks a collapse: Customer Operations (a third of the group) fell 8.1 to 5.9 while every other function held or improved. 'Above target, near sector median' is true and misleading.
embedded_issues.expected: Decompose the weighted mean. State that the group-level dip reads as noise but is entirely attributable to one function (excluding Customer Operations the group scores ~8.1), so the 'steady' framing is wrong. Stronger answers also pull the shift split (day 6.5 / night desk 4.7) and note the night desk's low participation makes its true position likely worse, not better.

embedded_issues.title: Overall attrition (11.2%, 'in line with sector') hides the concentration: 24 of 35 Q2 leavers are Customer Operations, 22 of 35 sit in the 1–3-year band, and the run-rate in that function is rising quarter on quarter.
embedded_issues.expected: Join the two leaver tables rather than reading them separately. State that the sector-range headline conceals a localised retention problem concentrated in one function and one tenure band, and cost it (backfill and time-to-proficiency) rather than leaving it as a count.

embedded_issues.title: Three exit verbatims from different leavers independently describe the same night-desk pattern: roster favouritism and worsened shifts after complaints. The roster-level data points at one team lead's roster group. No formal grievance exists — which is itself a signal.
embedded_issues.expected: Connect the verbatims to each other and to the leaver data (night desk 15 of 24 CO leavers; Roster C 11 of those; rostering moved to team-lead discretion in January). Treat it as a serious, specific line of inquiry — and handle the named-individual dimension with due-process care: an investigation with natural justice, not a verdict in a briefing note.

inquiry_quality.description: How well the candidate used the Halcyon Knowledge System to interrogate the data rather than accept the summary. Scored on the quality and progression of inquiry, not the count of questions.
indicators: Asks for the per-function breakdown behind the headline (surfaces the 5.9)
Asks what the group looks like excluding Customer Operations, or otherwise tests the average
Asks for shift-level or roster-level cuts (surfaces the night desk and Roster C)
Asks for leaver detail that joins function and tenure, or the quarter-on-quarter trend
Checks the caveats: participation by shift, exit-interview sample, benchmark provenance
Frames questions to retrieve and test evidence, not to solicit a verdict or have the system author the note

recommendations.description: Quality of the recommended actions: specific, sequenced, proportionate to the evidence, and sensitive to the people involved.

rubric.20-25: Targeted and sequenced: an immediate, confidential review of night-desk rostering with scheduling moved back to transparent rules while it runs; a properly-handled management inquiry (due process for the team lead, protection from retaliation for staff); a retention response aimed at the 1–3-year Customer Operations population; and a fix for the measurement gap (participation, roster-level items). Owns the recommendation and names the risk of doing nothing.
rubric.13-19: Right direction but partial — e.g. targets Customer Operations but stays at 'listening sessions and manager training', or surfaces the roster issue without an implementable, fair process for it.
rubric.6-12: Generic HR playbook (focus groups, engagement action plans, comms refresh) applied to the whole group; no targeting, no sequencing, no ownership.
rubric.0-5: No meaningful recommendation, or actions that follow the dashboard framing ('continue to monitor').

professional_communication.description: Whether the note serves a director walking into an executive meeting: leads with the finding, separates evidence from inference, is honest about uncertainty, and handles the sensitive material with judgement.

rubric.12-15: Reads like a real briefing note: headline finding first, evidence tightly marshalled, inference labelled as such, sensitive names handled with care, clear asks. Fits the time available.
rubric.8-11: Competent and clear but list-like or unprioritised; the reader must do some of the work.
rubric.4-7: Restates data without a line of argument, or buries the finding; tone or structure would not survive an executive reading.
